title: Three years in orbit
lede: From launch to the warehouse in about three years. Filter by thread.

events.title: Suspension patent filed
events.text: Bush Boake Allen Inc. files a U.S. patent application titled Method of suspending inclusions, about keeping solid pieces afloat in beverages. Whether it covers Orbitz is not in our sources.

events.title: Launch
events.text: Clearly Canadian introduces Orbitz, a fruit drink with suspended gel balls, aimed at 12- to 17-year-olds.

events.title: Introduced around the country
events.text: Orbitz is introduced around the country, Science World says in October.

events.title: Arizona test market
events.text: A University of Arizona summer paper lists Orbitz among the summer’s test-market beverage launches.

events.title: The bottle test
events.text: Science World leaves a bottle alone for a few days. The spheres sink part of the way and stop.

events.title: “A lava lamp you can drink”
events.text: An Associated Press feature takes Orbitz national; the company expects a million cases by year end.

events.title: Two stars
events.text: The Spokesman-Review’s panel tastes it: $1.09 a bottle, 130 calories.

events.title: Canadian launch
events.text: Clearly Canadian announces the Canadian launch. Sales start May 1 at 7-Eleven, Shoppers Drug Mart and Famous Players cinemas.

events.title: “Orbitz is hot”
events.text: The Washington Post reports it has captured a niche among young people.

events.title: $9.4M
events.text: Orbitz sales in the first half of 1997.

events.title: A question for rheologists
events.text: Two participants in a University of Minnesota short course ask how gel particles up to 5 mm across stay suspended in Orbitz.

events.title: Planet Orbitz prelude
events.text: An Internet Archive capture of orbitz.com shows the Orbiterium prelude, with a choice of Netscape or Internet Explorer routes.

events.title: Patent suit settled
events.text: FundingUniverse’s company history says a patent suit by Bush Boake Allen, a raw-material supplier for Orbitz, is settled with a licensing fee.

events.title: Distribution bought back
events.text: The same history says Clearly Canadian buys back distribution rights in several key Mid-Atlantic states. It now controls its North American distribution.

events.title: $1.46M
events.text: First-half 1998 sales are down almost 85%.

events.title: “Expected life-cycle”
events.text: The marketing chief says the decline was planned for; new drinks are coming.

events.title: Yield stress published
events.text: The Rheology Bulletin prints the answer to the Minnesota question. The liquid has a yield stress of 0.04 Pa.

events.title: Discontinued
events.text: Orbitz is no longer made.

events.title: Sales suspended
events.text: The same history says Orbitz sales were suspended because of dwindling sales, with a significant writedown.

events.title: A parked address
events.text: A domain-service placeholder replaces the drink’s site at orbitz.com.

events.title: Orbitz, LLC named
events.text: FundingUniverse’s Orbitz, Inc. history says the airline-backed travel venture is officially named Orbitz, LLC and Orbitz, Inc.

events.title: ©2000 Orbitz, LLC
events.text: orbitz.com carries a ©2000 Orbitz, LLC notice.

events.title: Parent shrinks
events.text: Clearly Canadian’s revenue is $20.5M, down from $34.9M in 1998.

events.title: New president
events.text: Clearly Canadian names Brent Lokash president, replacing chief executive Douglas Mason, who is to continue in an active role.

events.title: Orbitz in the past tense
events.text: A press release describes Orbitz, in the past tense, as a drink with gel spheres that seemed to defy gravity.

events.title: ORBITZ application filed
events.text: Clearly Canadian files a U.S. trademark application for ORBITZ covering soft drinks, non-carbonated fruit-flavored beverages and energy drinks.

events.title: Snack maker bought
events.text: Clearly Canadian says it has acquired DMR Food Corporation, an organic and natural snack-food company in Eastern Canada.

events.title: Application abandoned
events.text: The ORBITZ application, allowed on May 6, 2008, is abandoned. The maker filed neither a statement of use nor an extension request in time.

events.title: Creditor proposal
events.text: Clearly Canadian files a proposal under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act. Creditors approve it on April 1, and the Supreme Court of British Columbia on April 26.

events.title: Khan acquires the company
events.text: Fast Company reports that the entrepreneur Robert R. Khan acquired the Clearly Canadian company this year.

events.title: Another ORBITZ filing
events.text: A different applicant, an individual, files ORBITZ DEFY GRAVITY DRINK ORBITZ for beverages, then abandons it on request on May 9.

events.title: No machines
events.text: A company representative says it no longer has the equipment to make Orbitz.

events.title: Registrations revoked
events.text: The SEC declares final an order revoking the registrations of each class of Clearly Canadian Beverage Corp.’s registered securities.

events.title: Full production resumes
events.text: Clearly Canadian resumes full-scale production, Fast Company says.

events.title: Trademark and machine sold
events.text: The old owners sold the trademark, and the machine that made the spheres was sold off for parts, Fast Company reports.
